item.title: Chat Uploads That Outlive the App
item.description:
The interview prompt: “Design media upload for a WhatsApp-style chat.” A user picks a 40MB video, sees a thumbnail with a progress ring, then switches to another app to take a call. iOS suspends your app, and may terminate it under memory pressure. When they come back, the video is sent. Nothing in that sentence is hard until the app leaves the foreground.

Here is the instinct most candidates reach for, and it is the wrong tool:

item.title: The Chat Outbox for Offline Sync
item.description:
The interview prompt is one line: “Design WhatsApp-style offline messaging for iOS.” You tap send on the subway, the message shows a clock, and three stops later it turns into a double tick. Simple to describe. The whole problem lives in what has to be true for that tick to be honest.

Here is the version most candidates draw first:

final class MessageQueue {
 private var messages: [Message] = []
 func enqueue(_ m: Message) { messages.append(m) }
 func dequeue() -> Message? { messages.isEmpty ? nil : messages.removeFirst() }
}

Spot the two bugs before reading on. One loses messages. The other duplicates them. By the end you will have the outbox and the client-side dedup key that kill both, and a status machine that can only move forward.

item.title: The reduce That's Secretly O(n²)
item.description:
map, filter, and reduce get recommended as the faster choice over a for loop. They do read better. Faster is the part that does not hold up, and one of them has a default that turns a one-line accumulation into O(n²) while sailing through review. By the end you will know which one, why, and the one-word change that fixes it.

“Functional is faster” is backwards

A for loop over an array is about as cheap as computing gets: one pass, one array, no intermediates. A chain of higher-order functions does the same logical work and allocates along the way.

item.title: How Closures Capture, and Why Your Screen Leaks
item.description: Push a screen, pop it, push it again, and watch deinit never fire while memory climbs. That is the most common memory bug in iOS, and it almost always comes down to one thing a closure does quietly: capture. A closure grabs the things it references and keeps them alive. Get that wrong with a closure that outlives the call, and you have a view controller that can never deallocate.

item.title: Copy-on-Write, and When Structs Bite
item.description:
“Use structs by default” is advice so repeated that nobody asks the obvious follow-up: what does the copy actually cost? Everyone can recite that structs copy and classes share. The part worth your attention is what “copy” means at runtime, when it is free, when it quietly is not, and the class of bug that shows up when you have lost track of which one you are holding.

We will assume you know the textbook difference. Assign a struct, you get an independent copy. Assign a class, both names point at the same instance. Here is everything past that.

item.title: What Swift's Optional Really Is
item.description:
How many states can a screen actually be in, and does its type let it represent states that mean nothing? That question is where optionals stop being about syntax.

Everyone meets Optional once, as “the box that might be empty,” then moves on to unwrapping. The parts that still bite years in are elsewhere: what Optional actually is, the two or three places it behaves in ways that surprise people, and the design call nobody frames at the syntax stage. When is an optional the right tool, and when is it a sign the problem has not been modeled yet?

item.title: Modeling the Current User Without a Global Singleton
item.description:
Almost every app has the line. User.current, or Session.shared, or AppState.user. A global you can reach from anywhere that holds the logged-in user. It is the most convenient object in the codebase on day one and, a year later, the most coupled. The profile module is usually where the rot shows up first, because profile screens read and write the current user more than anywhere else.

The real question is not what goes in the UserProfile module. It is how the current user gets modeled and reached, because that one decision is what keeps the app testable or slowly strangles it.

item.title: Architecture for a Team Scaling 5 to 20
item.description: When a team is five people, architecture is a technical question. When it is twenty, it is mostly an organizational one, and the codebase will end up shaped like the org chart whether you plan for it or not. That last part is Conway’s law, and on a growing iOS team it stops being a fun aphorism and starts being the thing that decides whether your release train runs on time.

item.title: Using Cursor in a Flutter Workathon
item.description:
Forty-eight hours to rebuild a real production screen in Flutter, test it, and ship it for a panel review. Nine teams. We wrote about 10,000 lines in two days, let Cursor generate roughly 80% of it, and placed 2nd.

The score is not the interesting part. What breaks when you lean on an AI agent under real time pressure, on code with deeply nested logic, while making decisions fast, is. Every item below cost us time before it saved us any. What follows is the workflow we ended up with, and why each piece earned its place.

item.title: The Shared Module Trap in iOS Apps
item.description:
You change one line in Core and the whole app recompiles. Again. The feature modules were the easy half of modularization and they came out fine. The half quietly eating the payoff is the shared module: the Core, Common, or Shared target everything depends on.

It starts as obvious good sense (“don’t duplicate networking”) and ends as a second monolith wearing a module’s clothes. It fails in a few specific, predictable ways. Name them and the fix is a small set of structural rules, with a concrete payoff: that one-line change stops rebuilding the whole app.

item.title: What Modular iOS Actually Costs
item.description:
“Should we modularize the app?” gets argued like a values question, monolith for the scrappy, modules for the grown-ups. It is not a values question. Modularization buys specific things and costs specific things, both measurable, and the teams that get burned are the ones that paid the cost without checking whether they needed what it bought.

The usual pros-and-cons list (“easier to scale”, “more complex setup”) is too vague to decide with. Price it out instead.

item.title: Why UIKit Breeds Massive View Controllers
item.description:
Every iOS team eventually fights the same file. A view controller that started small and is now four figures of line count, the one nobody volunteers to touch. The usual explanation is discipline: someone got lazy, nobody refactored. That explanation is comfortable and mostly wrong.

Massive View Controller is not a discipline failure. It is what UIKit’s design pushes you toward by default. Understand the mechanism and you stop fighting symptoms. First, why the controller becomes a magnet. Then what each escape hatch actually costs, because none of them are free.

Everything about Error Handling in Combine

In the previous article, while discussing the 5 essential caveats to remember to master Combine, we touched upon error handling briefly. In this article, we will dive deep into error handling in Combine, covering everything there is about built in error handling in Combine.

Whether you’re a seasoned developer or eager to learn, this series will provide the insights and skills needed to master these powerful frameworks. Let’s get started.

item.title: Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember
item.description:
Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember

Combine framework’s caveats: Learn key pitfalls and actionable insights for effective integration into your code.

Combine, Apple’s own reactive programming framework, holds immense potential. However, effectively using its capabilities demands one to be aware of specific caveats and pitfalls.

This article explores these caveats and provides actionable insights for integrating Combine effectively into your code. While some considerations here may seem intuitive, they are often overlooked until you grasp Combine thoroughly.
